passage:
Sunday night
The community book fair is over and my first thought on the walk home was: total failure. Forty people came instead of the two hundred we hoped for. The children's corner ran out of chairs. It rained at four.
Then I caught myself. "Total" is a big word. Alka always asks me to score things out of ten, so I sat down with tea and did it.
Honest score: five out of ten.
What worked: the storytelling hour was full. We sold ninety books. Three new volunteers signed up. The old librarian cried when a girl asked for poetry.
What didn't: posters went up too late. No shelter plan for rain. Too few chairs.
Next time: posters two weeks earlier, a tarpaulin, borrow chairs from the temple hall.
Five out of ten doesn't feel like failure. It feels like a first try.
Francis

qa.a: Alka would likely feel pleased that the scoring habit helped, and could add ideas to the list for the next fair.

Class teacher's note, winter term, by Pema
December, cold morning. During homework check, Bhavna went white. Her maths notebook was at home. Before I reached her desk, she was sobbing. "Please don't tell Papa. He'll be so angry. I'll be sent to hostel. Everyone will call me the girl who got expelled."
She had forgotten homework once all term.
I took her outside and asked her the worst thing she was imagining, then, "And what do you think will really happen?" She thought, then whispered, "You'll say bring it tomorrow?" "Yes." Her breathing slowed.
What I did next: at pickup I told her mother gently how frightened she had been, and we agreed to practise the "what will really happen" question at home.

Saturday, 11:40 pm
I messaged Santosh at 4 about the cycling trip. "Coming tomorrow?" Two grey ticks. Delivered. Not read.
It's been seven hours and forty minutes.
First I thought he was busy. Then I thought, he's annoyed about Thursday, when I didn't pass him the ball. Then I thought, he's told everyone. Then I thought, that's why nobody replied to my photo on the group chat either. By ten I was sure: the whole class is sick of me and they're making plans without me.
I know how it sounds. But every step feels real in my chest, like it already happened.
Mummy came in and asked why I was awake. I told her. She said, "Santosh's family went to his nani's village today. Didn't you hear? No signal there." I didn't know.
I still feel shaky. But the story in my head just got a big hole in it.
Chetan

passage:
When I was in Class 5, our school did an Onam pageant, and Chetan sir chose who would be Mahabali. I wanted it so badly. I practised the walk at home with a bedsheet cape. He chose Anoop.
I decided right away: Chetan sir thinks I'm useless. I even told Amma, "He doesn't like me, that's why." I didn't have one reason. It just felt true, so I said it like a fact.
I sulked the whole festival. At the pageant I didn't even clap.
Two weeks later, Chetan sir asked me to read the welcome speech for the district inspector. I was so confused. Later I found out Anoop was chosen because he was the tallest and the costume only fit him.
I still remember how sure I was, with zero proof.
— Kishore

qa.q: Why was Anoop chosen to be Mahabali?
qa.a: Anoop was chosen because he was the tallest and the costume only fit him.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after not being chosen, and why did the belief seem true?
qa.a: Kishore felt hurt and jealous, and that strong feeling made the idea that the teacher thought Kishore was useless feel like a fact.

qa.q: What could Kishore have done instead of deciding what Chetan sir thought?
qa.a: Kishore could have asked Chetan sir why Anoop was chosen, and would have heard about the costume.

qa.q: What would change if Kishore had known about the costume from the start?
qa.a: Kishore might still have felt disappointed, but would not have sulked through Onam believing the teacher disliked them.

grounding: A child looks back on being sure, with no evidence, that a teacher thought them useless after not being chosen for an Onam pageant.

passage:
It was the first week back after the holidays, and I was wearing my cousin's old jacket, the brown one with a torn pocket. In chemistry, I saw Omkar and Sahil whispering and looking my way. I just knew it. They were laughing at the jacket. I could practically hear them: "Where did he get that, a museum?" My face went hot. I zipped the jacket up and then took it off and stuffed it in my bag, even though the lab was cold.
All day I avoided them. At lunch I ate on the stairs.
In the evening, Omkar messaged: "Hey, Sahil and I were saying we should ask you to join our quiz team. You in?"
I read it four times. They were looking at me because they were talking about me. Just not what I thought. I'd heard a whole conversation that nobody had actually said.
— Thomas

qa.q: What did Omkar's message ask Thomas to join?
qa.a: It asked Thomas to join their quiz team.

qa.q: Why was Thomas so sure the whisper was about the jacket?
qa.a: Thomas felt self-conscious and embarrassed about the old jacket, so the fear filled in the words, as if they were spoken aloud.

qa.q: What could Thomas try the next time it feels certain that people are mocking?
qa.a: Thomas could remember that nobody can hear thoughts, or simply ask, "What's up?" before deciding what they meant.

qa.a: Omkar would probably be surprised and a bit sorry, since they were planning to invite Thomas.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9B, by Sudha
Damini refused to come back into the classroom after the break today. I found her by the water cooler, eyes red. She said, "Anu and Keya were laughing at my salwar. It's old and faded." I asked what they had said. "They didn't have to say anything. They looked at me and whispered and laughed. I know what they were thinking."
I asked, "What exactly did you hear?" She was quiet. "Nothing. But I know."
I didn't tell her she was wrong, because I don't know either. I said, "You might be right, and you might not. Right now you're treating a guess as something they said."
What I did next: with her permission, I asked Anu casually what was so funny at break. Anu showed me a video of her dog falling off a sofa. I told Damini. She laughed, embarrassed, and came back to class.

qa.q: What did Anu show Sudha?
qa.a: Anu showed a video of her dog falling off a sofa.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling by the water cooler, and why?
qa.a: Damini felt humiliated and hurt, certain the girls were laughing at her faded salwar, though she hadn't heard a word.

qa.q: How did Sudha handle Damini's certainty?
qa.a: Sudha didn't dismiss her, asked what she actually heard, and then, with permission, checked quietly with Anu.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had checked with Anu?
qa.a: Damini might have kept avoiding the girls and felt ashamed of her clothes, believing an insult that never happened.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager certain classmates mock her clothes, treating imagined thoughts as spoken words, until she checks.

passage:

I hate Thursdays now. Jasleen and Kiran were whispering in the back row and they both looked at me. Right at my kurta. The yellow one Mummy stitched. I know they think it looks homemade and cheap. Kiran even covered her mouth. I could hear exactly what they'd be saying: "Look at her, she thinks she's so stylish."
For the whole class I sat with my dupatta over the embroidery.
But diary, if I'm honest, I didn't hear a single word. Not one. I made up the whole thing and then believed it like they'd shouted it.
Tomorrow I'm going to do something scary. I'm going to ask Jasleen, "What were you two laughing about?" If it was my kurta, at least I'll know. If it wasn't, I've wasted a whole evening feeling awful.
Neelam

passage: Uma, beti, you think Nikhil is angry with you because he was quiet at dinner? Let your Sudha Masi tell you something. When I was nineteen, in nursing college, I came back from a twelve-hour ward shift. My friends were planning a Sunday picnic at the lake. I sat in the corner, eyes half closed, saying nothing. Kamala said loudly, "Look at Sudha's face. She clearly hates the plan." Everyone turned to me. I felt so misread. My first wish was to snap back. But I was too tired even for that. So I said softly, "I don't hate it. I'm just so tired I can't think. Ask me tomorrow." Kamala laughed and said, "Oh! I thought you were angry." Next day I helped plan the whole thing. So ask Nikhil, beti. Don't decide his face for him.

qa.q: What had Sudha just come back from?
qa.a: She had come back from a twelve-hour ward shift.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel when Kamala said she clearly hated the plan?
qa.a: She felt misread and stung, with a wish to snap back, since she was only exhausted, not angry.

qa.q: What choice in the story cleared up the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Sudha softly said what she was actually feeling, tired not angry, and asked them to check the next day.

qa.q: How might Kamala have felt once Sudha explained?
qa.a: Kamala seemed relieved and a bit sheepish, laughing that she had thought Sudha was angry.

grounding: An aunt recalls being told she clearly hated a plan when she was only exhausted, and gently saying what she actually felt.

passage: The bus to the trek base broke down at Mandi in pouring rain, and the seven friends sat in a roadside dhaba waiting for a mechanic. Harsha had written two exams that week and slept four hours on the overnight train. He sat with his hood up, staring at his chai. Farhan was planning out loud. "We'll start at five, do the ridge by noon." Harsha said nothing. Farhan stopped. "Harsha, you obviously hate this plan. Just say it." The others looked over. Harsha felt his face heat up. He didn't hate it. He hadn't even heard half of it. He took a breath. "I'm not angry, yaar. I'm wiped out. Two exams and no sleep. The plan's fine. I just need to sleep before I can care about ridges." Farhan's shoulders relaxed. "Oh. Okay. Want my jacket as a pillow?" Harsha put his head on the table.

qa.q: Where did the bus to the trek base break down?

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when Farhan said he obviously hated the plan?
qa.a: Harsha felt misread and embarrassed, his face heating up, since he was only exhausted, not against the plan.

qa.a: He calmly said what was really going on, two exams and no sleep, so Farhan could stop guessing.

grounding: A tired friend is told he obviously hates the trek plan, feels misread, and gently explains that he is exhausted, not angry.

passage: Bhupen came off a double shift at the café in Pune with coffee on his sleeves and ringing ears. Swati was already on his sofa with three friends, planning a trip to a music festival. "Bhupen! Look at these dates!" He nodded and sank into the chair. "Mm." Swati kept talking. Tickets, trains, where to stay. He stared at the ceiling fan. "Okay, what's wrong?" Swati put her phone down. "You clearly hate the idea. You've been making that face since you came in." Bhupen felt something twist in his chest. Now he had to defend a face. "I don't hate it," he said slowly. "I've been on my feet for fourteen hours. I'm not against the festival. I'm against standing up." Swati burst out laughing. "Why didn't you say?" "I just did." She tossed him a cushion and moved the planning to the next day.

qa.q: How many hours had Bhupen been on his feet?
qa.a: He had been on his feet for fourteen hours.

qa.q: What did Bhupen feel when Swati said he clearly hated the idea?
qa.a: Bhupen felt misread and frustrated, something twisting in his chest at having to defend a face.

qa.q: What worked in how Bhupen answered?
qa.a: He said slowly and gently what was really true, that he was exhausted, not against the festival, which cleared it up quickly.

qa.q: How might Swati see Bhupen's silence before he explained?
qa.a: Swati read his tired face as disapproval, perhaps because she was excited and wanted him to share it.

grounding: A tired young man is told by a friend that he clearly hates the trip plan and gently says he is exhausted, not angry.

passage: At the hospital billing office, Kashish had been sure since morning that Yash was annoyed with her. He'd said "okay" without looking up when she asked for the discharge files. He hadn't joined the tea break. In her head she'd already written the conversation: he thought she'd taken credit for the new filing system; he'd complained to the supervisor; he'd never trust her again. By two o'clock she'd replayed it thirty times. Then she remembered her own rule. She walked to his desk. "Yash, is something wrong? With me, I mean?" He looked up, confused. "With you? No. My tooth has been killing me since last night. I can barely talk." He pointed to his swollen cheek. Kashish almost laughed with relief. "Go to the dental OPD downstairs. I'll cover your files." Five hours of imagined arguments, gone in two minutes.

qa.q: What was wrong with Yash, according to Yash?
qa.a: His tooth had been killing him since last night, and he could barely talk.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel once Yash explained?
qa.a: Kashish felt relieved, almost laughing, after hours of imagined conflict.

qa.q: What is the useful habit in this passage?
qa.a: Asking directly "Is something wrong?" instead of guessing, which replaced hours of made-up conversation with a two-minute answer.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt about Kashish's question?
qa.a: Yash was surprised and probably grateful, especially when Kashish offered to cover his files.

grounding: An adult sure a colleague is annoyed asks directly instead of guessing, and a two-minute question replaces hours of imagined dialogue.

passage:
Dear Sonali,
You'll laugh at this. Remember I told you my new manager, Mr Kurien, seemed annoyed with me? Short replies, no smiley in his emails, walked past my desk without saying hi. I spent the whole weekend imagining it. He thought my presentation was weak. He regretted hiring me. He was going to put me on a performance plan. I wrote imaginary replies in the shower.
On Monday I tried what you once told me: just ask. I knocked on his door and said, "Is something wrong with my work? I'd rather hear it directly." He looked genuinely puzzled. "Your work is fine. I've been dealing with a family thing. I'm sorry if I seemed short." It took two minutes. Two minutes, versus a whole weekend of arguments with someone who wasn't even arguing with me.
Thank you for the advice.
Farhan

qa.a: Farhan's new manager, Mr Kurien.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel over the weekend, and what shows it?

grounding: An adult writes to a friend about being sure a manager was annoyed, then asking directly and replacing a weekend of guessing with two minutes.

passage: So this was last year, at the bank branch where I work. I'm Nilesh, by the way. There was this colleague, Suraj, who sat opposite me. One Monday, he just stopped talking to me. Didn't say good morning, didn't share his tiffin. I went home and lay awake building a whole case. He must be upset that I got the Friday half-day. Or that I joked about his cricket team. Or maybe someone told him something about me. By Wednesday I was avoiding him at the water cooler and rehearsing speeches in my head. Then on Thursday I got so tired of it that I just walked over and said, "Suraj, have I done something? You seem off with me." He blinked. "What? No. My father's in hospital. I'm barely sleeping." I felt terrible and relieved at the same time. Three days of stories, all wrong. I sat with him at lunch that day, and just listened.

qa.q: What did Suraj say when Nilesh asked?
qa.a: He said his father was in hospital and he was barely sleeping.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel after hearing Suraj's answer?
qa.a: Nilesh felt terrible and relieved at the same time, sorry for Suraj and relieved it wasn't about anything Nilesh had done.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who is building a case like Nilesh did?
qa.a: Ask the person directly and kindly early on, as Nilesh finally did, instead of spending days on stories.
